q: Which agency enforces federal rules against false advertising?
r: The Federal Trade Commission
It polices unfair and deceptive practices.

q: What does the Securities and Exchange Commission require of public companies?
r: Regular, accurate financial disclosures
Investors need reliable information.
w: The SEC does not set prices.
Employment of a set number of workers

q: What is deregulation?
r: Reducing government rules that apply to an industry
Supporters hope it will boost competition.
w: Adding more rules to an industry

q: What is a common argument for regulating pollution?
r: Firms ignore costs they push onto others
Regulation makes polluters bear the cost.
w: Pollution raises company profit for everyone
Clean air is a private good
Clean air is a shared resource.

q: A carbon tax is designed to:
r: Make polluters pay for the harm they cause
It builds the cost of pollution into prices.

q: What is a tradable pollution permit?
r: A right to emit a set amount that can be bought and sold
It creates a market for cutting pollution.
w: A fine for emitting any pollution
A free pass to pollute without limit

q: What is a government-provided public good?
r: National defense
It benefits everyone and cannot easily be denied.

q: Why might the government give a subsidy to a positive externality such as vaccination?
r: Society gains more than the buyer alone gets
A subsidy raises use toward the efficient level.

q: What is the main purpose of an excise tax on tobacco?
r: Raise revenue and discourage use
The tax raises the price of the good.
w: It is a small part of revenue.

q: What is a user fee?
r: A charge for using a government service
Park entrance fees are an example.
w: A tax paid by every citizen equally
A fine for breaking the law

q: What does the Federal Trade Commission do about mergers?
r: Reviews those that might reduce competition
It can challenge deals that harm buyers.
w: Sets the price of merged firms' goods

q: What was the purpose of the Sherman Antitrust Act?
r: Break up monopolies and ban price fixing
It was passed in 1890.

q: What is a patent?
r: Exclusive rights to an invention for a set time
It rewards innovation.
w: Exclusive rights to a brand name
A license to open a store

q: Why do patents sometimes create temporary monopolies?
r: Only the holder may sell the invention for a time
The holder can charge higher prices.
w: Patents let any firm copy the invention
Patents set price ceilings by law
They expire after a set time.

q: What is a copyright?
r: The legal right to control copies of an original work
It covers books, music and software.
w: It is a right, not a tax.
A license to sell goods abroad
A guarantee of a work's quality

q: What does the Fair Labor Standards Act regulate?
r: Minimum wage and overtime
It also limits child labor.

q: What does the Occupational Safety and Health Act aim to do?
r: Keep workplaces safe and healthy
Employers must reduce hazards.
w: It does not set insurance prices.
Limit the number of workers hired

q: What does the Americans with Disabilities Act require of employers?
r: Reasonable accommodations for qualified workers
It bars disability discrimination.
w: It does not require higher pay.

q: What is a government contract?
r: An agreement for a firm to supply goods or services to government
It can be a big source of business.

q: How do government purchases affect GDP?
r: They are a component of total spending
G is one part of C + I + G + NX.

q: What is the multiplier effect of government spending?
r: Spending can raise total output by more than its own size
It circulates as income to others.
w: Spending has no effect on income

q: What is the federal minimum wage meant to do?
r: Set a floor for pay under the law
It aims to protect low-wage workers.
w: Cap how much any worker can earn
It sets a floor, not a cap.

q: What is a tariff's usual effect on domestic producers?
r: It shields them from foreign competition
Imports cost more, so home goods look cheaper.
w: It exposes them to more foreign competition
It sets their prices by law
It does not set their prices.

q: What is a quota's usual effect on the price of an imported good?
r: It tends to rise
Limited supply raises the price.
w: Less supply tends to raise price.

q: What is nationalization?
r: The government taking ownership of a private industry
The state runs it afterward.
w: A firm selling shares to the public
A firm moving to another country
A firm merging with a competitor

q: What is privatization?
r: Selling government-owned assets to private owners
Governments may privatize to raise cash or efficiency.
w: The state taking over a private firm
A firm going out of business

q: What does real GDP adjust for?
r: Changes in the price level
It shows output in constant prices.

q: Nominal GDP rises 6% while prices rise 2%. About how much did real GDP grow?
r: 6% minus 2% is about 4%.

q: What is a GDP deflator?
r: A price index that covers all goods in GDP
It converts nominal GDP to real GDP.
w: A tool that lowers a company's taxes
It is not a tax tool.

q: What does the Consumer Price Index track?
r: Prices of a basket of goods households buy
It is a main measure of inflation.

q: The CPI was 250 last year and is 260 this year. What was the inflation rate?
r: 10 divided by 250 equals 0.04.
w: That treats the point change as a percent.

q: Why is core inflation useful?
r: It leaves out volatile food and energy prices
It shows the underlying trend.
w: It counts only food and energy

q: What is the labor force participation rate?
r: The share of working-age people who are working or looking
It shows how engaged people are in the labor market.
w: The share of workers who are unemployed
The share of workers in unions
The share of jobs that are full time

q: Why might the unemployment rate fall even if no new jobs appear?
r: Discouraged workers leave the labor force
They are no longer counted as unemployed.
w: More people join the labor force
That tends to raise the rate.
That does not change the count.

q: What is the underemployment problem?
r: Workers hold jobs below their skills or hours wanted
They are counted as employed but want more.
w: Workers have no jobs at all

q: What is a leading indicator?
r: A statistic that tends to change before the economy does
Building permits are an example.
w: A statistic that changes after the economy does
A statistic made up by a leader

q: What is a coincident indicator?
r: A statistic that moves with the economy at the same time
Industrial production is an example.
w: A statistic that moves before the economy does
A statistic that moves long after the economy
A statistic that has no timing

q: Which is generally a lagging indicator?
r: The unemployment rate
It reacts after the economy changes direction.

q: What does a rising consumer confidence index suggest?
r: Households may spend more
Optimism supports demand.
w: Confidence usually moves the other way.

q: What does the Index of Leading Economic Indicators try to do?
r: Signal turning points in the business cycle
It combines several forward-looking measures.

q: What is the trade deficit?
r: Imports exceeding exports in value
The country buys more than it sells abroad.
w: A fall in the exchange rate

q: A country exports $400 billion and imports $450 billion. What is its trade balance?
r: A deficit of $50 billion
$400 billion minus $450 billion equals -$50 billion.

q: What does the current account measure?
r: A country's trade in goods and services plus income flows
It records money moving across borders.
w: The money in a person's checking account
The number of firms in the country

q: What is a recession's effect on tax revenue?
r: It typically falls
Incomes and profits drop.

q: What does a yield curve compare?
r: Interest rates on bonds with different maturities
An inverted curve is often seen as a warning.

q: What does an inverted yield curve often signal?
r: A higher chance of a coming recession
Short-term rates exceed long-term rates.
w: It is usually seen as a warning.

q: What is the personal savings rate?
r: The share of disposable income that households save
A higher rate means more saving.
w: The interest rate on savings accounts
The share of income paid in taxes
The share of spending on housing

q: What is retail sales data used to show?
r: How much consumers are spending at stores
It signals the strength of demand.
w: How many stores close each year
How much stores pay in rent

q: What does the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) gauge?
r: The health of manufacturing and service activity
Readings above 50 suggest expansion.

q: What is the difference between a tariff and a quota?
r: A tariff taxes imports; a quota limits their amount
Both restrict trade.
w: A tariff limits imports; a quota taxes them

q: What is an export subsidy?
r: Government support that makes exports cheaper abroad
It helps domestic exporters compete.

q: Why do economists often oppose export subsidies?
r: They distort trade and cost taxpayers
Other countries may retaliate.
w: They lower prices at home for sure

q: What is the main benefit of comparative advantage?
r: Countries gain by trading what they produce at lower opportunity cost
Both sides can end up with more.
w: One country gains only at another's expense
All countries must make every good
Trade removes the need for specialization

q: In one hour Country X makes 4 shirts or 2 tools; Country Y makes 3 shirts or 3 tools. Who has the comparative advantage in shirts?
r: Country X
X gives up 0.5 tool per shirt; Y gives up 1.
w: Y has a higher opportunity cost for shirts.

q: What does a trade surplus imply about a country's net exports?
r: They are positive
Exports exceed imports.

q: What is a floating exchange rate?
r: A rate set by supply and demand in currency markets
It changes continually.
w: A rate fixed by the government
A rate set by a company

q: What is a fixed (pegged) exchange rate?
r: A rate a government holds at a set value
It may buy or sell currency to defend it.
w: A rate set by market forces
A rate that changes every minute

q: If demand for the euro rises relative to supply, what happens to its value?
r: It appreciates
Higher demand lifts the price of the currency.

q: A weaker home currency tends to make exports:
r: Cheaper for foreign buyers
Foreigners need less of their money to buy.

q: What is the World Bank's main focus?
r: Financing development projects in poorer countries
It lends for long-term development.

q: What does the International Monetary Fund do?
r: Supports monetary cooperation and lends to countries in financial trouble
It also monitors global finances.

q: What is the European Union's single market?
r: A market allowing free movement of goods, services, people and capital
Members share common rules.
w: A market limited to one country

q: What is the USMCA?
r: A trade agreement among the United States, Mexico and Canada
It replaced NAFTA.
w: It is not a military pact.

q: What is a customs union?
r: Members drop tariffs among themselves and share one outside tariff
The EU works this way for goods.
w: Members keep separate tariffs for each other
That is a free trade area.
Members share a single currency only

q: What is a trade war?
r: Countries raising tariffs on each other's goods in turn
It can hurt both sides.
w: A fight with weapons over trade routes
A dispute inside a single company
That is not a trade war.
A festival of imports and exports
That is not a trade war.

q: What is dumping?
r: Selling goods abroad below their cost or home price
It can trigger anti-dumping duties.
w: Selling goods at a fair price

q: What is the infant industry argument?
r: New industries need protection until they can compete
Temporary tariffs may help them grow.
w: Old industries must be shut down
Babies need to be protected from imports
All industries should be taxed more

q: What is a common criticism of the infant industry argument?
r: Protection may last too long and keep inefficient firms alive
Firms may never become competitive.
w: It removes all costs for consumers
It forces firms to export more

q: What is a multinational enterprise?
r: A firm that operates in several countries
It has branches or subsidiaries abroad.
w: A firm limited to one city
A union of workers across borders

q: What is a trade-off of globalization for workers?
r: Cheaper goods but possible job losses in some industries
Gains and losses are unevenly spread.
w: Higher prices and more jobs for everyone
That is not the usual result.
No change in jobs or prices
Lower wages for every worker without exception
